## Closing Synthesis
edits.after:
The last ayah makes that even clearer. Once others turn away from truth, the believer's heart is not supposed to become enslaved to their refusal. It is supposed to settle in Allah as Mawla and Nasir.

### What the Commentators Actually Disagreed About

It would be dishonest to hand you one reading of *hatta la takuna fitnah* as though the tradition only ever had one. It had at least two, and knowing both matters before anyone quotes this verse at you.

The reading this reflection has been working with — *fitnah* as the persecution that pressures a believer out of his religion — is the one Ibn Kathir preserves from al-Zuhri and 'Urwah ibn al-Zubayr through Muhammad ibn Ishaq. Al-Tabari carries something close to it from Ibn Jurayj, who joins the two ideas: *that no believer be persecuted away from his religion, and that tawhid be purely for Allah with no shirk in it*. Al-Tabari also records al-Hasan glossing *fitnah* here as *bala'*, affliction. And al-Tabari places under this very verse the long letter of 'Urwah to 'Abd al-Malik, which narrates the Meccan persecution of the early Muslims and ends by saying that this was the situation in which *wa qatiluhum hatta la takuna fitnah* was revealed.

But that is not the majority reading, and it is not al-Tabari's own. His verdict is wider and blunter: *fight them until there is no shirk, and none is worshipped but Allah alone with no partner, so that the affliction is lifted from Allah's servants on the earth* — and then he says it plainly, **that is the fitnah**. Behind that he stacks the same gloss from Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Suddi. Ibn Kathir puts the identical reading under his own heading for the passage and names Abu al-'Aliyah, Mujahid, al-Rabi' ibn Anas, Muqatil ibn Hayyan and Zayd ibn Aslam alongside it. Al-Muyassar glosses *fitnah* here as shirk together with turning people away from the path of Allah. Al-Jalalayn glosses it in a single word: *shirk*.

So of the four commentaries consulted for this reflection, every one carries the shirk reading, and only Ibn Kathir also carries the persecution reading. Presenting the second as the plain sense of the verse, without saying that, would be exactly the quiet trimming a reader is right to resent.

Al-Tabari records a second dispute on the tail of the same verse. Some read *fa-ini intahaw*, "but if they desist," as desisting from *fighting*. Al-Tabari prefers "if they desist from shirk," and he gives his reason: in his view, even if the idolaters ceased fighting, fighting them remained obligatory upon the believers until they entered Islam. That is his position, stated in his own words, and it is reported here rather than hidden — a reader who meets it later in al-Tabari should not feel this page kept it from him. It is reported, not endorsed and not refuted.

There is one more voice, and it is the strongest thing in this reflection's own favour. Al-Bukhari records — and Ibn Kathir quotes it at length — that a man pressed Ibn 'Umar to fight, citing this exact verse at him. Ibn 'Umar answered: "We did that during the time of the Messenger of Allah, when Islam was weak and the man would be tried in religion, either tormented to death or being imprisoned. When Islam became stronger and widespread, there was no more Fitnah." Asked on another occasion what *fitnah* even referred to, he said the Prophet ﷺ was fighting the idolaters and at that time simply living among them was itself a trial in religion — "It is nothing like what you are doing, fighting to gain leadership!"

That is not this reflection's wish imposed on the text. It is a Companion who lived through the revelation, locating the *fitnah* in the persecution of that moment and refusing to let the verse be borrowed for a contest over power. Both narrations are al-Bukhari's.

None of this settles a ruling, and none of it is meant to. This is a tadabbur: it reads what the passage says and reports where the commentators divided — over what *fitnah* names here, and over what "if they desist" refers to. Those are questions of law with long histories and conditions attached, and they belong to qualified scholars, not to a reflection.

## Closing Synthesis

And there is a word the classical sources use for this change that a reflection should not step around: *naskh*, abrogation. Ibn Kathir states it flatly — one Muslim was to endure ten, and "Allah abrogated this part later on, but the good news remained." ### Theme 2: The Demand Came Down; the Word for Who Wins Did Not

The other striking lesson is about telling apart what changed from what did not.

What changed is real, and the commentaries are not shy about it. The ratio came down from one-against-ten to one-against-two, and the measure of endurance being asked for came down with it. Ibn 'Abbas says so; al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir both carry him saying it.

Sabr appears in both verses — *sabirun* qualifying the twenty, *sabirah* qualifying the hundred.
Allah's permission still governs the outcome.

That means divine relief is not permission for inward slackness. It is merciful recalibration so that real steadfastness can continue. We often misread lightening as downgrading. The Qur'an presents it as wise mercy that preserves the path instead of breaking the people on it.

### What the Commentators Actually Disagreed About

Everything above is contemplation. But this passage also carries a ruling, and the ruling has a history the reader is owed before treating the numbers as something binding on him personally.

Start with what the ratio was taken to govern. Ibn Kathir keeps the good news of the verse in view — a few can overcome many. But the commentaries also read the ratio as a rule about **fleeing**. Al-Tabari records 'Ata', 'Ikrimah, Mujahid and al-Dahhak all saying that under the first ratio a Muslim was not permitted to flee from ten, and under the second he is not permitted to flee from two.

Then the consequence, which both Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari attach and which is easy to miss. In the report Ibn Ishaq carries from Ibn 'Abbas, preserved in both editions, the rule cuts in two directions: once the Muslims stood at half their enemy's number they were not allowed to withdraw from them, and if they were fewer than that, "they were not obligated to fight the disbelievers and thus allowed to avoid hostilities." The second half is a permission, not a demand.

Then the harder disagreement: was the first ratio ever a binding obligation at all? Al-Tabari holds that it was, and his argument is structural — the verse is phrased as a statement but functions as a command, and the proof is the word *takhfif* itself, since there is no lightening except after a weight. Al-Jalalayn frames it the same way, *khabar bi-ma'na al-amr*, a statement carrying the force of a command. Al-Dahhak says outright that it was obligatory. And yet al-Tabari also preserves, without suppressing it, a report from Ibn 'Abbas saying the opposite: it "was not a command Allah resolved upon them nor made obligatory; rather it was an exhortation and a counsel." That same report then turns sharply on people who were using the arithmetic as an excuse to stay out of fighting altogether — which shows the ratio being argued in both directions inside the tradition itself.

There is even disagreement over *why* the lightening came. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir mostly tie it to the hardship and the weakness the verse names. But Ibn 'Abbas is also recorded saying the first ratio belonged to a time "when the Muslims were few," and that the easing came when they became many — which is how al-Jalalayn puts it too, *lamma kathuru*.

So there is real ikhtilaf here on more than one question: whether the first ratio bound, what the second one binds, what it permits, and what occasioned the change. Those are matters of law, with conditions, contexts and qualifications that no reflection can supply.

Which is the last thing to say plainly: this is a tadabbur, not a fatwa. It reads two verses and reports where the commentators divided. Nothing on this page is a ruling about fighting, and nothing on it should be carried into a question about fighting. For that, ask a qualified scholar.

## Closing Synthesis
